title: Ubiquity
abstract: From its invention to the internet age, photography has been considered universal, pervasive, and omnipresent. This anthology of essays posits how the question of when photography came to be everywhere shapes our understanding of all manner of photographic media. Whether looking at a portrait image on the polished silver surface of the daguerreotype, or a viral image on the reflective glass of the smartphone, the experience of looking at photographs and thinking with photography is inseparable from the idea of ubiquity—that is, the apparent ability to be everywhere at once. While photography’s distribution across cultures today is undeniable, the insidious logics and pervasive myths that have governed its spread demand our critical attention, now more than ever.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

Ubiquity has found its clearest impact in teaching and use: the record shows four YouTube instances discussing the book and 3,549 downloads through OAPEN. Those signals suggest that the book is being read and encountered beyond its initial publication context, even though the formal citation record is still at an early stage.

Full narrative

Published by Leuven University Press in 2021, Ubiquity is an open-access scholarly book by Jacob W. Lewis and Kyle Parry that examines photography as a pervasive medium across historical and digital contexts. The subject profile in the record centers on photography, visual arts, art history, portrait, mythology, and literature, which fits the book’s interdisciplinary approach to how photographic media are understood and experienced.

The strongest evidence of impact comes from usage and pedagogical uptake. OAPEN reports 3,549 downloads, indicating sustained reader interest in the book. In addition, the teaching-adoption signals identify four YouTube videos in which the book is discussed, supporting the interpretation that Ubiquity has circulated as a pedagogical or discussion resource rather than remaining only a library item.

The publication also appears in an open-science and access-oriented infrastructure. OpenAIRE records the work as open access in a hybrid status, and the presence of peer-review metadata through PRISM adds a further marker of formal scholarly publishing processes. Funding acknowledgements point to support from KU Leuven, the Liz Warnock Publication Fund at Northwestern University, and the Arts Research Institute at the University of California, Santa Cruz, which is consistent with a collaboratively supported academic publication.

By contrast, the citation record is still minimal, with OpenAlex showing zero citations at the time captured here. That does not diminish the book’s usage or instructional presence; it simply means the scholarly citation trail has not yet developed in the available record. Overall, Ubiquity shows early and recognizable reach through downloads and teaching-related discussion, with the current evidence pointing more to readership and classroom or public intellectual use than to citation-based scholarly uptake.
